title: India's Young Astronomers Shine With Four Golds and a Silver in Hanoi
excerpt: All five Indian students medalled at the 19th International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics, placing India joint third among 64 countries in the biggest IOAA ever held.
body:
• All five Indian students won medals at the 19th International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics in Hanoi: four golds and one silver.
  • Gold medallists: Pranjal Dixit (Hyderabad), Sumant Gupta (Delhi), Akshat Srivastava (Gurugram) and Arnav Sehrawat (Faridabad). Harshil Amitkumar Patel (Vadodara) won silver.
  • India placed joint third with host Vietnam in the medal tally, behind Iran and South Korea, who each swept all five golds. With 307 students from 64 countries, this was the largest IOAA ever held.
  • For parents eyeing the Olympiad path: India's national selection and training is run by the Homi Bhabha Centre for Science Education (HBCSE-TIFR) through its multi-stage National Olympiad Programme. Every Indian student across all five senior science Olympiads this year won gold or silver — a first since 1989.

India's school astronomy talent put on its finest display yet at the 19th International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics (IOAA), held in Hanoi, Vietnam, from September 25 to October 5. All five members of the Indian team returned with medals — four golds and one silver — as the country finished joint third with host nation Vietnam in the medal tally, according to the Homi Bhabha Centre for Science Education (HBCSE), a National Centre of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai.

A perfect five

The gold medallists are Pranjal Dixit of Hyderabad, Telangana; Sumant Gupta of Delhi; Akshat Srivastava of Gurugram, Haryana; and Arnav Sehrawat of Faridabad, Haryana. Harshil Amitkumar Patel of Vadodara, Gujarat, won the silver medal. The result continues a remarkable run for India: over the last five years, every Indian student at the astronomy Olympiad has won either gold (64 per cent) or silver (36 per cent).

This year's competition was the biggest IOAA to date, with 307 students from 64 countries. In all, 51 gold, 48 silver and 60 bronze medals were awarded. Iran and South Korea topped the table, with each country's team winning all five golds.

"A historic season for Indian science The astronomy result closes out a landmark year for India at the international science Olympiads."

Not an easy test

The IOAA is not a school quiz. The competition has three components — theory, observation and data analysis — and this year's theoretical problems would strain most undergraduates. Students had to solve problems involving the motion of an object around the Lagrange (L1) point, estimate the mass ejected by the star Betelgeuse during its famous "Great Dimming" event, and grapple with stellar nucleosynthesis, solar neutrino detection, Einstein's rings and gravitational delay, the physics of Jupiter's interior, and superluminous galaxies in the early universe.

India's relationship with the Olympiad is a long one. Since Indian participation began in 1999, 49 per cent of Indian students at astronomy Olympiads have won gold, 35 per cent silver and 13 per cent bronze. The country's pipeline is run by HBCSE, the national nodal agency for India's science and mathematics Olympiad programmes, which conducts the multi-stage selection and training process under the Department of Atomic Energy.

A historic season for Indian science

The astronomy result closes out a landmark year for India at the international science Olympiads. With this event, all five senior-level Olympiads of the year — mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and astronomy — have concluded, and every Indian student has won either gold (16 students) or silver (8 students), a first since India began participating in international Olympiads in 1989.

Earlier in the season, India recorded clean sweeps at both the International Physics Olympiad (five golds, joint world No. 1) and the International Chemistry Olympiad (four golds, joint world No. 1), and collected 12 gold and seven silver medals across physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics. Department of Atomic Energy Secretary and Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Dr Ajit Kumar Mohanty described the season's results as a source of national pride, reflecting the dedication of students and mentors and decades of institutional support for young scientific talent.

Why this resonates with the diaspora

For Indian-American and diaspora families, stories like this land differently. The Olympiad pipeline that produced this haul is one diaspora parents increasingly try to plug into — HBCSE's open training and selection process is the entry point, and alumni of these teams routinely go on to top research universities and labs worldwide, including in the United States. Each medal is also quiet evidence that India's investment in school-level science is paying off at the highest global benchmark — a narrative that resonates with the large share of the diaspora that built its careers on that same education system.

What's next

The 2026 Olympiad season is now complete, and attention will turn to the 2027 cycle, when HBCSE begins the next round of national selections. Iran and South Korea remain the benchmarks — both took perfect five-gold teams to Hanoi this year — and catching them will require India's pipeline to keep producing at this level. If 2026 is any indication, it will.
